title: Poison at the river
hookLine: the cousins grow up under one roof, and envy grows with them until it reaches for poison
carry: matsarya: envy, one of the six enemies
tomorrow: a girl, a sage's mantra, and the rising sun.

cards: A fruit tree in a royal garden, boys up in its branches reaching for fruit. Below stands Bhima, the second son of Pandu. He kicks the trunk, and the boys come tumbling down with the fruit.
In the water he holds his cousins under until they gasp. In the dust he drags them by the hair. The Mahabharata says he meant no malice; it was a boy's play.
But one of the boys on the ground is Duryodhana, the eldest son of Dhritarashtra. And he doesn't forget.

teach.b: The story moves fast now. Madri has twin sons, Nakula and Sahadeva. In Hastinapura, Gandhari's sons are born, Duryodhana the eldest.

In the forest, Pandu dies. Sages bring Kunti and the five brothers to Hastinapura, and two families of cousins share one palace. Bhima beats them all, and Duryodhana, the story says, burns with jealousy.
So he holds a day of water games by the Ganga, poisons Bhima's food, ties him as he sleeps, and pushes him into the river.
Bhima sinks to the realm of the Nagas, the serpent people. Their bites work against the poison, the Naga king welcomes him, and he comes home stronger.
Vidura tells Kunti to say nothing in public, for her other sons' sake. Hindu teachers have a name for what grew in Duryodhana.
The tradition counts six inner enemies: desire, anger, greed, moha, which we met with his blind father, pride, and matsarya, envy.
Matsarya is the pain of watching someone else have what you want. Notice it doesn't start as poison. It starts with a boy on the ground under a fruit tree, watching his cousin win.
Fed every day, it grows into a plan. The tradition calls it an enemy because it lives inside you and fights you. Today it's a cousin's acceptance letter, a friend's post, a sibling praised at dinner.
The feeling comes. The question is whether you feed it.

how: Many Hindus honor serpents on Nag Panchami with milk and prayers, and some families tell the Mahabharata to children a piece at a time; Bhima among the Nagas is one of the pieces told.

o: the serpent people below the waters who saved Bhima
the river spirits who carried Bhima's poison away
the poison Duryodhana put into Bhima's food

games.q: the cousins at play — tap the pairs.
p: their venom worked against the poison
envy, one of the six enemies

s: the text says Bhima bullied his cousins out of hatred
the text says he meant no malice; it was a boy's play. the grudge grew on the other side.
matsarya, envy, is one of the six inner enemies
with desire, anger, greed, moha and pride; they're called enemies because they fight you from inside.
Kunti accused Duryodhana before the whole court
she spoke her fear to Vidura, and he told her to keep quiet to protect her other sons.

games.q: your cousin gets the summer program you wanted and the family can't stop praising her. by Duryodhana's story, what's wise?
o: name it, matsarya, and wish her well before it grows.
say nothing, and quietly keep score.
point out her flaws so the praise evens out.
games.why: Duryodhana's envy started small, under a fruit tree, and he fed it until it became poison. name the enemy early, and meet her joy with friendliness.

practice: The Yoga Sutra, an old Hindu guide to the mind, offers a cure: meet the happy with friendliness. Bring to mind someone who has something you wanted. Notice the sting, and name it: matsarya.
Then wish them well, once, plainly: may it go well for you. If you pray, ask God's blessing on them. If you don't, just let the wish stand.

wordCard.voice: Naga, the serpent people below the waters, whose venom worked against the poison envy put in Bhima's food.

orig.note: Sanskrit nāga: a serpent; in the story, the serpent people whose realm lies below the waters.

carryVoice: Your line: matsarya, envy, one of the six enemies. It started under a fruit tree. Tomorrow, a secret older than all the cousins.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (the Pandavas brought to Hastinapura; Bhima's play; the poisoning at the Ganga; Bhima among the Nagas; Vidura's counsel to Kunti)
